idiom_name: std::function<R(Args...)> storing a lambda or function object
implementation_notes: C++ replaces the classic callback interface with a callable value: a lambda or function object is passed where the callback is expected, and std::function<R(Args...)> provides the type-erased, storable, invocable wrapper for deferred callbacks (C++11; std::move_only_function adds move-only targets in C++23). Capture is the context mechanism - the closure holds the per-operation state, so no void* plumbing is needed - and std::bind or std::ref attach extra arguments when the signature does not line up. An empty std::function throws std::bad_function_call when invoked, so the callable is a precondition or an explicit check. The classic abstract class survives only where a stable ABI or virtual interface with several methods is wanted (stream buffers, visitor-style interfaces).
pitfalls: A lambda capturing this keeps the object reachable from the closure; if the posted work outlives the object the callback dangles - capture by value or by weak handle instead.
std::function copies its target and may allocate; hot paths prefer a template parameter or std::move_only_function for move-only captures.
std::ref/std::cref inside std::bind store references, so the referenced object must outlive every invocation.
Throwing from a callback invoked inside a noexcept completion handler terminates the process (std::thread/Asio handlers are noexcept), so errors belong in the callback's own status argument.

variants.name: Template callable (compile-time, zero-overhead)
variants.idiom_name: function object (functor) or function pointer as a template parameter
variants.implementation_notes: Before C++11 added lambdas and std::function, and still whenever zero overhead matters, the callable is a template parameter: the service templates on the callback type and invokes it directly, exactly as the standard algorithms have taken comparator and predicate function objects since C++98. There is no type erasure, no allocation and no indirect-call penalty, and the C++11 named requirement Callable (INVOKE) later formalized what may be passed. Use this form when the callback type is known at the call site and the API can live in a header; take the classic virtual interface instead when the callback must cross a binary boundary, be chosen at run time, or sit in a non-template container.
pitfalls: Every instantiation is a distinct type: the callback type becomes part of the function's signature, so it cannot be stored in a non-template container and the implementation must be visible in the header.
The function object is copied into the request, so it must be copyable and cheap; a shared handler needs a pointer or reference_wrapper rather than a copy per request.
Without type erasure there is no run-time polymorphism - handlers selected from configuration or a registry need std::function, a function pointer, or a virtual interface.

variants.name: C++20 coroutines (co_await on an awaitable)
variants.idiom_name: co_await an awaitable completion / completion token
variants.implementation_notes: With C++20 coroutines the completion callback is replaced by suspension: the initiating coroutine co_awaits an awaitable that the operation resumes with the result, so the callback machinery hides inside the coroutine frame (this is how Boost.Asio's use_awaitable and completion-token overloads work). Choose it when the toolchain is C++20 and the callback chains are long enough that the flattened control flow pays for the coroutine frame; keep plain callbacks where the completion must cross a C ABI or a callback-only library boundary, and note that a completion token slot can offer callbacks, futures and co_await for the same operation.
pitfalls: A coroutine frame outlives the calling function: pointers or references into the caller's stack become dangling after the first suspension, so parameters must be captured by value.
An awaitable that resumes twice, or never, corrupts the coroutine state machine - single completion is the contract to enforce at the boundary with callback-based code.
Forgetting to keep the returned task alive (dropping it without running to completion) silently cancels the operation.
